**Rishi Sunak**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-4) (born 12 May 1980) is a British politician who served as [Prime Minister of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") and [Leader of the Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_\(UK\) "Leader of the Conservative Party \(UK\)") from 2022 to 2024. He previously served as [Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer "Chancellor of the Exchequer") from 2020 to 2022 under [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson"), and briefly served as [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_\(United_Kingdom\) "Leader of the Opposition \(United Kingdom\)") from July to November 2024 following his defeat in the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"). Sunak has been the [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_\(United_Kingdom\) "Member of Parliament \(United Kingdom\)") (MP) for [Richmond and Northallerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_and_Northallerton "Richmond and Northallerton"), previously [Richmond (Yorks)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_\(Yorks\) "Richmond \(Yorks\)"), since 2015.
Sunak was born in [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton") to [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indians "British Indians") parents who immigrated to Britain from East Africa in the 1960s. He was educated at [Winchester College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_College "Winchester College") and then studied [philosophy, politics and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy,_politics_and_economics "Philosophy, politics and economics") at [Lincoln College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_College,_Oxford "Lincoln College, Oxford"), and earned a [Master of Business Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Business_Administration "Master of Business Administration") degree from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in California as a [Fulbright Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulbright_Scholar "Fulbright Scholar"). During his time at Oxford, Sunak joined the Conservatives. After graduating, he worked for [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs") and later as a partner at two [hedge fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_fund "Hedge fund") firms. Sunak was elected to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"). As a [backbencher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backbencher "Backbencher"), he supported the successful campaign for [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit") in the [2016 European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 European Union membership referendum"). He was appointed to the junior ministerial position of [Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Under-Secretary_of_State_for_Local_Government "Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government") by [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") in 2018 and was appointed to the [cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Kingdom "Cabinet of the United Kingdom")-attending role of [Chief Secretary to the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Secretary_to_the_Treasury "Chief Secretary to the Treasury") by Johnson in 2019.
In 2020, Sunak was promoted to Chancellor of the Exchequer. During [his time in the post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellorship_of_Rishi_Sunak "Chancellorship of Rishi Sunak"), Sunak was prominent in the [government's financial response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_government_response_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic "British government response to the COVID-19 pandemic") to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom") and its [economic impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"), including the [furlough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_Job_Retention_Scheme "Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme") and [Eat Out to Help Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eat_Out_to_Help_Out "Eat Out to Help Out") schemes and the [cost-of-living crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_cost-of-living_crisis "United Kingdom cost-of-living crisis"). As chancellor, Sunak received high approval and popularity ratings in the early stages of the pandemic, although his popularity later declined amid the cost-of-living crisis of 2022. He resigned as chancellor in July 2022 amid [a government crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_2022_United_Kingdom_government_crisis "July 2022 United Kingdom government crisis"), and lost the subsequent [party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July%E2%80%93September_2022_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "July–September 2022 Conservative Party leadership election") to [Liz Truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Truss "Liz Truss") that September. After spending the whole duration of the [premiership of Liz Truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Liz_Truss "Premiership of Liz Truss") on the backbenches, Sunak was elected unopposed in the [leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2022_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "October 2022 Conservative Party leadership election") to succeed Truss the following October; aged 42 at the time he became prime minister, Sunak became the youngest prime minister since [the Earl of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Earl_of_Liverpool "The Earl of Liverpool") in 1812.
During [his premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Rishi_Sunak "Premiership of Rishi Sunak"), Sunak attempted to improve the economy and stabilise national politics. He outlined five key priorities: halving [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation"), growing the economy, cutting debt, reducing [National Health Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service "National Health Service") waiting lists, and stopping [small-boat crossings of the English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel_migrant_crossings_\(2018%E2%80%93present\) "English Channel migrant crossings \(2018–present\)") by enacting the [Rwanda asylum plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda_asylum_plan "Rwanda asylum plan"). On foreign policy, Sunak authorised [foreign aid and weapons shipments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "United Kingdom and the Russian invasion of Ukraine") to [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") in response to the [Russian invasion of the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine"), and pledged support for [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") after the [7 October attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_October_attacks "7 October attacks") and subsequent [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") whilst later [calling for a ceasefire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calls_for_a_ceasefire_during_the_Gaza_war "Calls for a ceasefire during the Gaza war") in the [Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_Strip "Gaza Strip"). He was unable to avert further unpopularity for the Conservatives, reflected in the party's poor performances in the [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2023 United Kingdom local elections") and [2024 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2024 United Kingdom local elections"). Sunak called a general election for July 2024 despite being widely expected to call the election in the autumn; the Conservatives lost this election in a landslide to the opposition [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_\(UK\) "Labour Party \(UK\)") led by [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer"), ending 14 years of Conservative government.
After leaving the prime minister's office, Sunak became Leader of the Opposition and remained Conservative leader for nearly four months while the [leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Conservative_Party_leadership_election_\(UK\) "2024 Conservative Party leadership election \(UK\)") to replace him took place, and formed a [shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Rishi_Sunak "Shadow Cabinet of Rishi Sunak"). He was succeeded by [Kemi Badenoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemi_Badenoch "Kemi Badenoch"), his [Shadow Housing Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_Housing,_Communities_and_Local_Government "Shadow Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government"). He remains a backbench MP, and may take some outside work that is publicly reported. In 2025 he also took a position as a part-time senior advisor with one of his previous employers, [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"), with some limits on his [lobbying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying "Lobbying") abilities.
## Early life and education (1980–2001)
Rishi Sunak was born on 12 May 1980 at the [Southampton General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton_General_Hospital "Southampton General Hospital") in [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton"), in [Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire "Hampshire"), England,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Hooker-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-6) to [East African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa")-born [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_people "Indian people") parents.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Sunak_Print-8) Sunak's family are [Punjabi Hindus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjabi_Hindus "Punjabi Hindus").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-rishis-10) Rishi is the eldest of three siblings.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-11) His brother is a psychologist and his sister works in New York as chief of strategy and planning at Education Cannot Wait, the United Nations Global Fund for Education in Emergencies and Protracted Crises.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Edwardes-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-13)
His father was born in the [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony") in 1949,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Sunak_Print-8) and was a general practitioner in the [National Health Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service "National Health Service") (NHS).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-DailyEcho2022-14) Sunak's mother was born in the [Tanganyika Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_Territory "Tanganyika Territory") (modern-day [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania")), and was a pharmacist who owned the Sunak Pharmacy in Southampton between 1995 and 2014, and has a degree from [Aston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_University "Aston University").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Tatler-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-16) Sunak's grandparents were born in the [Punjab Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Punjab "British Punjab") of [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_India "British India") and [migrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_diaspora_in_Southeast_Africa "Indian diaspora in Southeast Africa") to [British protectorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_protectorate "British protectorate") in East Africa, prior to the [Partition of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India") in 1947. His paternal grandfather, Ramdas Sunak, migrated from [Gujranwala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujranwala "Gujranwala") in [West Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Punjab "West Punjab") to [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") in 1935. His maternal grandfather, Raghubir Berry, was born in [Ludhiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana "Ludhiana") in [East Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Punjab "East Punjab"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-17) and moved to [Dar es Salaam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dar_es_Salaam "Dar es Salaam") as an engineer.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Sunak_Print-8)

## Career
### Business career (2000–2015)
Following an internship in 2000, Sunak worked as an analyst for investment bank [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs") between 2001 and 2004.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-whoswho-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Business-25) He then worked for [hedge fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_fund "Hedge fund") management firm [The Children's Investment Fund Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Children's_Investment_Fund_Management "The Children's Investment Fund Management") (TCI) from September 2006 to November 2009.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-27) He left the fund to join former colleagues in California at a new hedge fund firm, Theleme Partners, which launched in October 2010 with $700 million under management.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-30) At both hedge funds, he directly reported to [Patrick Degorce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Degorce "Patrick Degorce").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-The_Guardian_Feb_2020-31) Sunak was a director of the investment firm Catamaran Ventures, owned by his father-in-law, the Indian businessman [N. R. Narayana Murthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N._R._Narayana_Murthy "N. R. Narayana Murthy") of [Infosys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infosys "Infosys"), between 2013 and 2015.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Business-25)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-32)
### Backbencher (2015–2018)
Sunak was selected as the Conservative candidate for [Richmond (Yorks)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_\(Yorks\) "Richmond \(Yorks\)") in October 2014.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-34) The seat was previously held by [William Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hague "William Hague").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-35) In the same year Sunak was head of the [Black and Minority Ethnic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_and_Minority_Ethnic "Black and Minority Ethnic") (BME) Research Unit of the conservative think tank [Policy Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_Exchange "Policy Exchange"), for which he co-wrote a report on BME communities in the UK.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-PE-36) He was elected as MP for the constituency at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election") with a majority of 19,550 (36.2%).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-37) During the 2015–2017 Parliament he was a member of the [Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs_Select_Committee "Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Select Committee").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-parlbio-38)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Official_portrait_of_Rishi_Sunak_crop_2.jpg/250px-Official_portrait_of_Rishi_Sunak_crop_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Official_portrait_of_Rishi_Sunak_crop_2.jpg)Official MP portrait, 2017
Sunak supported the successful campaign to leave the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") in the [2016 European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 European Union membership referendum"), criticising the EU's immigration laws: "We are discriminating against countries with whom we have ties of history, language and culture"[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-leave-39) That year, he wrote a report for the [Thatcherite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thatcherite "Thatcherite") think tank [Centre for Policy Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Policy_Studies "Centre for Policy Studies") supporting the establishment of [free ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_ports "Free ports") after [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit"), and the following year wrote a report advocating the creation of a retail bond market for [small and medium-sized enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_and_medium-sized_enterprises "Small and medium-sized enterprises").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-42) Following Cameron's resignation, Sunak endorsed [Michael Gove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gove "Michael Gove") in the [2016 Conservative Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "2016 Conservative Party leadership election"), and later endorsed successful candidate [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") after Gove was eliminated in the second round of voting.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-44)
Sunak was re-elected at the [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_\(Yorks\)_\(UK_Parliament_constituency\)#Elections_in_the_2010s "Richmond \(Yorks\) \(UK Parliament constituency\)") with an increased majority of 23,108 (40.5%).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-45) In the same year, Sunak wrote a paper for Policy Exchange on the importance and fragility of the UK's undersea infrastructure.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-46) Sunak was re-elected at the [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election") with an increased majority of 27,210 (47.2%).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-47) Following boundary changes in the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"), Sunak won the seat of [Richmond and Northallerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_and_Northallerton "Richmond and Northallerton"), which replaced his former seat of Richmond (Yorks), with a majority of 23,059 (51.4).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-48)
### Local government under-secretary (2018–2019)
Sunak was appointed to a junior ministerial position in May's [second government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_May_ministry "Second May ministry") as [Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Under-Secretary_of_State_for_Local_Government "Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government") in the [2018 cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_British_cabinet_reshuffle "2018 British cabinet reshuffle").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-parlbio-38) Sunak voted for May's [Brexit withdrawal agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_withdrawal_agreement "Brexit withdrawal agreement") [on all three occasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_votes_on_Brexit "Parliamentary votes on Brexit"), and voted against a [second referendum on any withdrawal agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_referendum_on_the_Brexit_withdrawal_agreement "Proposed referendum on the Brexit withdrawal agreement"). May's withdrawal agreement was rejected by Parliament three times, leading to May announcing her resignation in May 2019.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-49)
Sunak supported [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson")'s successful bid to succeed May in the [2019 Conservative Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "2019 Conservative Party leadership election") and co-wrote an article with fellow MPs [Robert Jenrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jenrick "Robert Jenrick") and [Oliver Dowden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Dowden "Oliver Dowden") to advocate for Johnson during the campaign in June.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-51)
### Chief secretary to the Treasury (2019–2020)
Sunak was appointed to the senior cabinet role of [chief secretary to the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_secretary_to_the_Treasury "Chief secretary to the Treasury") by Johnson, serving under [Sajid Javid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajid_Javid "Sajid Javid").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-52) He became a member of the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_the_United_Kingdom "Privy Council of the United Kingdom") the next day.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-53) During the 2019 general election, Sunak represented the Conservatives in debates.
### Chancellor of the Exchequer (2020–2022)
Main article: [Chancellorship of Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellorship_of_Rishi_Sunak "Chancellorship of Rishi Sunak")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Rishi_Sunak_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Rishi_Sunak_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rishi_Sunak_\(cropped\).jpg)Sunak in a public information film about [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19"), April 2020
In the weeks leading up to [Johnson's first cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_British_cabinet_reshuffle "2020 British cabinet reshuffle") in February 2020, a number of briefings in the press had suggested that a new economic ministry led by Sunak might be established, to reduce the power and political influence of the Treasury.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-55) By February 2020, it was reported that Javid would remain in his role as Chancellor and that Sunak would stay on as Chief Secretary to the Treasury, in order to "keep an eye" on Javid.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-56)
On 13 February 2020, the day of the reshuffle, Javid resigned as chancellor, following a meeting with Johnson. During the meeting, Johnson had offered to allow Javid to keep his position on the condition that he dismiss all his advisers at the Treasury and replace them with ones selected by 10 Downing Street.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-JavResign-57) Upon resigning, Javid told the [Press Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_Association "Press Association") that "no self-respecting minister would accept those terms".[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-javidguardian-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-59) Sunak was promoted to chancellor to replace Javid as part of Johnson's first cabinet reshuffle later that day.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-JavResign-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-javidguardian-58)
#### COVID-19 pandemic
Further information: [British government response to the COVID-19 pandemic § Financial response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_government_response_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic#Financial_response "British government response to the COVID-19 pandemic")
In response to the first confirmed [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") cases in January 2020, Sunak introduced advice for travellers coming from affected countries in late January and February 2020, and began [contact tracing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_tracing "Contact tracing"), although this was later abandoned.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Kobie-60) There were further societal restrictions on the public as [the virus spread across the country in the following weeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"), initially resisting more stringent measures introduced elsewhere in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Europe "COVID-19 pandemic in Europe") and [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Asia "COVID-19 pandemic in Asia").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:9-61) On 23 March 2020, as [COVID-19 had become a pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") and began rapidly spreading across the country, Sunak became prominent in [the government's response to the pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_government_response_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic "British government response to the COVID-19 pandemic") and its [economic impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_impact_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"). On 20 March 2020, Sunak gave a statement on COVID-19, saying:[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-62)
> Now, more than any time in our history, we will be judged by our capacity for compassion. Our ability to come through this, won't just be down to what government or businesses do, but by the individual acts of kindness that we show each other. When this is over, we want to look back on this moment and remember the many small acts of kindness done by us and to us. We want to look back on this time and remember how we thought first of others and acted with decency. We want to look back on this time and remember how, in the face of a generation-defining moment, we undertook a collective national effort – and we stood together. It's on all of us.
#### Furlough scheme
Main article: [Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_Job_Retention_Scheme "Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Boris_Johnson_Covid-19_Presser_%2850462222663%29.jpg/250px-Boris_Johnson_Covid-19_Presser_%2850462222663%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boris_Johnson_Covid-19_Presser_\(50462222663\).jpg)Sunak at a press conference on COVID-19, October 2020
Sunak introduced a programme providing £330 billion in emergency support for businesses,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-63) as well as the [Coronavirus Job Retention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_Job_Retention_Scheme "Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme") [furlough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furlough "Furlough") scheme for employees. This was the first time a British government had created such an employee retention scheme.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-partington-65) The scheme was introduced on 20 March 2020 as providing grants to employers to pay 80% of a staff wage and employment costs each month, up to a total of £2,500 per person per month.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-partington-65) The cost was estimated at £14 billion a month to run.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-66)
The furlough scheme initially ran for three months and was backdated to 1 March. Following a three-week extension of the countrywide lockdown the scheme was extended by Sunak until the end of June 2020.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-68) At the end of May, Sunak extended the scheme until the end of October 2020. The decision to extend the job retention scheme was made to avoid or defer mass redundancies, company bankruptcies and potential unemployment levels not seen since the 1930s.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-69) In March 2021, Sunak announced that the scheme had been extended once more until September 2021.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-BBCFurlough2021-70)
#### Eat Out to Help Out
Main article: [Eat Out to Help Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eat_Out_to_Help_Out "Eat Out to Help Out")
In July 2020, Sunak unveiled a plan for a further £30 billion of spending which included a [stamp duty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_duty_in_the_United_Kingdom "Stamp duty in the United Kingdom") holiday, a cut to [value-added tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value-added_tax_in_the_United_Kingdom "Value-added tax in the United Kingdom") (VAT) for the hospitality sector, a job retention bonus for employers and the Eat Out to Help Out scheme,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-71)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-72) aimed at supporting and creating jobs in the [hospitality industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospitality_industry_in_the_United_Kingdom "Hospitality industry in the United Kingdom"). The government subsidised food and soft drinks at participating cafes, pubs and restaurants at 50%, up to £10 per person. The offer was available from 3 to 31 August on Monday to Wednesday each week.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-73) In total, the scheme subsidised £849 million in meals.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-74)
[Patrick Vallance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Vallance "Patrick Vallance") and [Chris Whitty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Whitty "Chris Whitty") were not informed of the scheme.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-75) Some considered the scheme to be a success in boosting the hospitality industry,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-76) whilst others disagreed.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-78) A 2020 study found that the scheme contributed to a rise in COVID-19 infection, which Johnson acknowledged but the Treasury rejected.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-bl-20201004-80)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-81) It was later said by Vallance during the [COVID-19 Inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_COVID-19_Inquiry "UK COVID-19 Inquiry") that Sunak had not informed medical advisers of the scheme until it was announced, whereas written evidence from Sunak said that the scheme had been discussed with medical advisers, including Vallance, and they had not objected.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-82)
#### Cost of living crisis and energy crisis
Main articles: [2021–present United Kingdom cost-of-living crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%93present_United_Kingdom_cost-of-living_crisis "2021–present United Kingdom cost-of-living crisis") and [2021 United Kingdom natural gas supplier crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_Kingdom_natural_gas_supplier_crisis "2021 United Kingdom natural gas supplier crisis")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Rishi_Sunak_Official_Cabinet_Portrait%2C_September_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Rishi_Sunak_Official_Cabinet_Portrait%2C_September_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rishi_Sunak_Official_Cabinet_Portrait,_September_2021_\(cropped\).jpg)Official cabinet portrait, September 2021
Amid the rising cost-of-living and energy crises, Sunak announced a £15 billion support package in May 2022, partly funded by a windfall tax on oil and gas producers that was expected to raise £5 billion.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-83) The package included a £400 energy-bill discount for households and a £650 payment for about eight million low-income households receiving means-tested benefits.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:4-84) Eligible pensioner households would receive an additional £300, while people receiving qualifying disability benefits would receive £150.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:4-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-85)
#### Budgets
Main articles: [2020 United Kingdom budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_Kingdom_budget "2020 United Kingdom budget"), [March 2021 United Kingdom budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_2021_United_Kingdom_budget "March 2021 United Kingdom budget"), and [October 2021 United Kingdom budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2021_United_Kingdom_budget "October 2021 United Kingdom budget")
[![Sunak in a dark blue suit standing in front of the black door of 11 Downing Street, holding a small red suitcase at arm's length.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Budget_Day_2021_%2851633616891%29.jpg/250px-Budget_Day_2021_%2851633616891%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Budget_Day_2021_\(51633616891\).jpg)Sunak holding the [budget box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_box_\(government\) "Red box \(government\)") the day of the [October 2021 budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2021_United_Kingdom_budget "October 2021 United Kingdom budget")
Sunak presented his first budget, Delivering on Our Promises to the British People, on 11 March 2020. It was scheduled to be followed by another budget in the autumn, but in September 2020 he announced that budget would be scrapped because of the COVID-19 pandemic, stating "now is not the right time to outline long-term plans – people want to see us focused on the here and now".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-86)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-87) Instead, additional statements were given by the chancellor in both [summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_2020_United_Kingdom_summer_statement "July 2020 United Kingdom summer statement") and [autumn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_2020_United_Kingdom_Winter_Economy_Plan "September 2020 United Kingdom Winter Economy Plan").
The Winter Economy Plan was delivered by Sunak on 24 September 2020. The purpose of the statement was to announce measures aimed at further helping to promote economic recovery following the impact of COVID-19. The plan aimed to further promote economic recovery while preserving jobs and businesses which were considered viable. After a [second lockdown in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Health_Protection_\(Coronavirus,_Restrictions\)_\(England\)_\(No._4\)_Regulations_2020 "The Health Protection \(Coronavirus, Restrictions\) \(England\) \(No. 4\) Regulations 2020") on 31 October 2020, the programme was extended several times, until 30 September 2021.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-BBCFurlough2021-70)
The July 2020 summer statement (also known as the coronavirus mini-budget) was delivered by Sunak on 8 July 2020. The purpose of the statement was to announce measures aimed at helping to promote economic recovery following the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The statement was delivered to the House of Commons, where Sunak unveiled a spending package worth £30bn. Concerns were subsequently raised by organisations including [HM Revenue and Customs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HM_Revenue_and_Customs "HM Revenue and Customs") and the [Institute for Fiscal Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Fiscal_Studies "Institute for Fiscal Studies") about the statement's impact, as well as its cost-effectiveness, while at least one major retailer declined to take advantage of a financial bonus scheme intended for rehiring employees placed on furlough during the pandemic.
In his March 2021 budget, Sunak emphasized the effect the COVID-19 pandemic has had on the economy, with 700,000 people losing their jobs, the economy shrinking by 10% (the largest fall in 300 years), and the highest borrowing outside wartime.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:5-88)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Part-89) The budget included an increase in the rate of corporation tax from 19% to 25% in 2023, a five-year freeze in the tax-free personal allowance and the higher rate income tax threshold, and the extension of the furlough scheme until the end of September.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-90) Sunak was the first Chancellor to raise the [corporation tax rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_corporation_tax "United Kingdom corporation tax") since [Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_\(UK\) "Labour Party \(UK\)")'s [Denis Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Healey "Denis Healey") in 1974.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Part-89)
In October 2021, Sunak made his third and final budget statement, which included substantial spending promises related to science and education.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-91) The budget increased in-work support through the [Universal Credit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Credit "Universal Credit") system by increasing the work allowances by £500 a year, and reducing the post-tax deduction taper rate from 63% to 55%.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-politics-20211027-92) £560 million of investment was announced for the [Levelling Up White Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levelling_Up_White_Paper "Levelling Up White Paper").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-93) Many of the announcements to be made in the budget were previewed before budget day, drawing criticism and anger from the House of Commons. In response to the criticism, Sunak said the budget "begins the work of preparing for a new economy".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-BBC_News-2021-94)
Sunak made what would ultimately be his final budget, his spring statement, on 23 March 2022. He cut [fuel duty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_duty "Fuel duty"), removed VAT on energy saving equipment (such as solar panels and insulation) and reduced national insurance payments for small businesses and, while continuing with a [planned national insurance rise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_and_Social_Care_Levy "Health and Social Care Levy") in April, he promised to align the primary threshold with the basic personal income allowance as of July. He also promised a reduction in [income tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_Tax_in_the_United_Kingdom "Income Tax in the United Kingdom") in 2024. Sunak also provided some funding which was intended to help vulnerable people cope with the cost of living.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-95)
#### Other actions
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Commemorative_coin_marking_Mahatma_Gandhi%E2%80%99s_remarkable_life_unveiled_for_the_first_time.jpg/250px-Commemorative_coin_marking_Mahatma_Gandhi%E2%80%99s_remarkable_life_unveiled_for_the_first_time.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commemorative_coin_marking_Mahatma_Gandhi%E2%80%99s_remarkable_life_unveiled_for_the_first_time.jpg)Sunak in November 2021, holding a [commemorative coin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commemorative_coin "Commemorative coin") of [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi")
Sunak hosted a [G7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G7 "G7") summit in London in June 2021.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-g7summit2-96) A tax reform agreement was signed, which in principle sought to establish a [global minimum tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_minimum_tax "Global minimum tax") on multinationals and online technology companies.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-g7summit2-96) In October 2021, the [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") signed an accord to join the tax reform plan.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-97) Later that month, Sunak attended [COP26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COP26 "COP26") in Glasgow.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-RSCO_12-98) During his speech given on 3 November, he said that he felt optimism despite daunting challenges and that by bringing together finance ministers, businesses and investors, COP26 could begin to deliver targets from the [Paris Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement "Paris Agreement").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-RSCO_22-99)
#### Resignation
Main articles: [Chris Pincher scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Pincher_scandal "Chris Pincher scandal") and [July 2022 United Kingdom government crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July_2022_United_Kingdom_government_crisis "July 2022 United Kingdom government crisis")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Chancellor_announces_additional_support_to_protect_businesses.jpg/250px-Chancellor_announces_additional_support_to_protect_businesses.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chancellor_announces_additional_support_to_protect_businesses.jpg)Sunak (right) pictured with [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") (left), March 2020
On 5 July 2022, Sunak and Javid resigned almost simultaneously amid a scandal surrounding the [sexual harassment allegations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Pincher_scandal "Chris Pincher scandal") against [Chris Pincher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Pincher "Chris Pincher"), which arose after it was revealed that Johnson had promoted Pincher to the position of Deputy Chief Whip while knowing of the allegations beforehand.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-100) Sunak was the second of 61 Conservative MPs to resign during the government crisis.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-resign22-101) He was succeeded as chancellor by Nadhim Zahawi.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-102) Following the resignations of Sunak and Javid, numerous junior ministers and parliamentary private secretaries also resigned,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-103) with many questioning Johnson’s honesty and integrity.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-104) More than 40 ministers and aides resigned on 6 July,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-105) a record for a 24-hour period, and Johnson announced his resignation as Conservative Party leader the following day.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-106) In his resignation letter Sunak said:
> The public rightly expect government to be conducted properly, competently and seriously. I recognise this may be my last ministerial job, but I believe these standards are worth fighting for and that is why I am resigning. It has become clear to me that our approaches are fundamentally too different. I am sad to be leaving Government but I have reluctantly come to the conclusion that we cannot continue like this.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-107)
  

### Conservative leadership bids
Main articles: [July–September 2022 Conservative Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July%E2%80%93September_2022_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "July–September 2022 Conservative Party leadership election") and [October 2022 Conservative Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2022_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "October 2022 Conservative Party leadership election")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Ready_for_Rishi_logo_-_blue.png/250px-Ready_for_Rishi_logo_-_blue.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ready_for_Rishi_logo_-_blue.png)Sunak's leadership bid logo
On 8 July 2022, Sunak announced his candidacy in the [leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/July%E2%80%93September_2022_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "July–September 2022 Conservative Party leadership election") to replace Johnson.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-108) Sunak launched his campaign in a video posted to social media, writing that he would "restore trust, rebuild the economy and reunite the country".[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-109) He said that his values were "patriotism, fairness, hard work",[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-110) and pledged to "crack down on gender neutral language".[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-111) During the campaign, Sunak pledged to included tax cuts only when inflation was under control, scrapping of the 5% VAT rate on household energy for one year, introducing a temporary £10 fine for patients who fail to attend GP appointments, capping of refugee numbers, and a tightening of the definition of asylum.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-112) On 20 July, Sunak and Foreign Secretary [Liz Truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Truss "Liz Truss") emerged as the final two candidates in the contest on 20 July to be put forward to the membership for the final leadership vote. He had received the most votes in each of the series of MP votes with Sunak receiving 137 to Truss's 113 in the final round.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-113) Sunak opposed Truss' economic plans and predicted they would result in economic damage, saying "Liz, we have to be honest. Borrowing your way out of inflation isn't a plan, it's a fairytale." A spokesperson for Sunak later said: "The reality is that Truss cannot deliver a support package as well as come good on £50bn worth of unfunded, permanent tax cuts in one go. To do so would mean increasing borrowing to historic and dangerous levels, putting the public finances in serious jeopardy and plunging the economy into an inflation spiral."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-114)
In the membership vote, Truss received 57.4% of the vote, making her the new leader.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-membervote-115) Sunak responded by offering his support to Truss, saying "It's right we now unite behind the new PM, Liz Truss, as she steers the country through difficult times."[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-116) He spent the duration of [Truss's premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truss's_premiership "Truss's premiership") on the backbenches. As Sunak predicted, Truss announced [large-scale tax cuts and borrowing in a mini-budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_2022_United_Kingdom_mini-budget "September 2022 United Kingdom mini-budget") on 23 September, which was widely criticised and – after it rapidly led to financial instability – largely reversed.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-117) She announced her resignation on 20 October 2022 amid [a government crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2022_United_Kingdom_government_crisis "October 2022 United Kingdom government crisis"), triggering a [leadership contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_2022_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "October 2022 Conservative Party leadership election").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-118) On 22 October, it was reported that Sunak had the required number of supporters—100 members of the House of Commons—to run in the ballot on 24 October. The total number of MPs who publicly declared support passed 100 on the afternoon of 22 October.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-119) On 23 October, Sunak declared that he would stand for election.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-120) After Johnson ruled himself out of the race and [Penny Mordaunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_Mordaunt "Penny Mordaunt") withdrew her candidacy, Sunak was announced as the new leader on 24 October.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-121)
## Premiership (2022–2024)
Main article: [Premiership of Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Rishi_Sunak "Premiership of Rishi Sunak")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Rishi_Sunak%27s_first_speech_as_Prime_Minister_Front.jpg/250px-Rishi_Sunak%27s_first_speech_as_Prime_Minister_Front.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rishi_Sunak's_first_speech_as_Prime_Minister_Front.jpg)Sunak delivering his first speech as Prime Minister, 25 October 2022
As the leader of the majority party in the House of Commons, Sunak was appointed as prime minister by [Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III "Charles III") on 25 October 2022, becoming the first [British Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Asian "British Asian") to take the office. At 42, Sunak became the youngest prime minister since [Robert Jenkinson, 2nd Earl of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Jenkinson,_2nd_Earl_of_Liverpool "Robert Jenkinson, 2nd Earl of Liverpool"), in 1812.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-122) In his first speech as prime minister, Sunak said that Truss "was not wrong" to want to improve growth and that he "admired her restlessness to create change", and added that "some mistakes were made", and that he was elected as party leader, and prime minister, in part to fix them.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:3-123) He said, "I will place economic stability and confidence at the heart of this government's agenda.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:3-123)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-124)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-125)
### Cabinet
Main article: [Sunak ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunak_ministry "Sunak ministry")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/The_formal_full_cabinet_portrait_%2853614511381%29.jpg/250px-The_formal_full_cabinet_portrait_%2853614511381%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_formal_full_cabinet_portrait_\(53614511381\).jpg)Sunak with [his Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunak_ministry "Sunak ministry"), 9 January 2024
Sunak selected his cabinet ministers after his appointment as prime minister. [Jeremy Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hunt "Jeremy Hunt") was appointed [Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer "Chancellor of the Exchequer"), and [Dominic Raab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Raab "Dominic Raab") was also re-appointed as deputy prime minister and Justice Secretary, he later resigned from these roles in April 2023 and was replaced by Oliver Dowden. [James Cleverly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cleverly "James Cleverly") was appointed [Foreign Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Secretary_\(United_Kingdom\) "Foreign Secretary \(United Kingdom\)") with [Suella Braverman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suella_Braverman "Suella Braverman") as [Home Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Secretary "Home Secretary"). [Ben Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Wallace_\(politician\) "Ben Wallace \(politician\)") was appointed [Secretary of State for Defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Defence "Secretary of State for Defence"). [Michael Gove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gove "Michael Gove") was appointed [Levelling Up Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levelling_Up_Secretary "Levelling Up Secretary"), [Grant Shapps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Shapps "Grant Shapps") was appointed as [Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Business,_Energy_and_Industrial_Strategy "Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy"), and Penny Mordaunt became Leader of the House of Commons and Lord President of the council. Other key appointments included [Simon Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Hart "Simon Hart") as [Parliamentary Secretary to the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Secretary_to_the_Treasury "Parliamentary Secretary to the Treasury") and [Chief Whip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Whip "Chief Whip") of the House of Commons, [Nadhim Zahawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadhim_Zahawi "Nadhim Zahawi") as [Chairman of the Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Conservative_Party "Chairman of the Conservative Party"), Oliver Dowden as [Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Duchy_of_Lancaster "Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster"), [Thérèse Coffey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9r%C3%A8se_Coffey "Thérèse Coffey") as [Environment Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Environment,_Food_and_Rural_Affairs "Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs"), [Mel Stride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Stride "Mel Stride") as [Work and Pensions Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_and_Pensions_Secretary "Work and Pensions Secretary") and [Mark Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Harper "Mark Harper") as Transport Secretary.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-126)
#### Reshuffles
Main articles: [February 2023 British cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_2023_British_cabinet_reshuffle "February 2023 British cabinet reshuffle") and [November 2023 British cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_2023_British_cabinet_reshuffle "November 2023 British cabinet reshuffle")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Prime_Minister%27s_Questions%2C_7_February_2024_06.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister%27s_Questions%2C_7_February_2024_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister's_Questions,_7_February_2024_06.jpg)Sunak speaking during [Prime Minister's Questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister's_Questions "Prime Minister's Questions"), 7 February 2024
Sunak's [first cabinet reshuffle in February 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_2023_British_cabinet_reshuffle "February 2023 British cabinet reshuffle") saw a significant restructuring of [government departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_the_Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Departments of the Government of the United Kingdom"). New departments included those for [Business and Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business_and_Trade "Department for Business and Trade"), [Energy Security and Net Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Energy_Security_and_Net_Zero "Department for Energy Security and Net Zero"), and [Science, Innovation and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Science,_Innovation_and_Technology "Department for Science, Innovation and Technology"). The [Department for International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_International_Trade "Department for International Trade") and the [Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business,_Energy_and_Industrial_Strategy "Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy") were split and merged into other departments. Ministers who joined the cabinet in the first reshuffle included [Greg Hands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Hands "Greg Hands") took over as chairman from Zahawi, though later resigned and replaced by [Richard Holden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Holden_\(British_politician\) "Richard Holden \(British politician\)"). [Lucy Frazer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Frazer "Lucy Frazer") became [Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Culture,_Media_and_Sport "Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport") taking over from Donelan. [Rachel Maclean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Maclean_\(politician\) "Rachel Maclean \(politician\)") left the backbenches and joined the [Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Levelling_Up,_Housing_and_Communities "Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-auto2-127)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-auto12-128) Sunak's [last cabinet reshuffle in November 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_2023_British_cabinet_reshuffle "November 2023 British cabinet reshuffle") saw the return of former prime minister David Cameron to government following a seven-year absence from frontline politics, replacing James Cleverly as foreign secretary. It also saw the departures of Braverman and Coffey from government and Hands from the cabinet, and the appointment of [Laura Trott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Trott_\(politician\) "Laura Trott \(politician\)") as [Chief Secretary to the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Secretary_to_the_Treasury "Chief Secretary to the Treasury").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:32-129)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-LifePeer2-130)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:0-131)
