In February 2023, Sunak negotiated a proposed agreement with the EU on [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland")'s trading arrangements which was published as the [Windsor Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_Framework "Windsor Framework").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-132) On 27 February, Sunak delivered a statement to the House of Commons, saying that the proposed agreement "protects Northern Ireland's place in our Union.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-133) On 22 March, the date of the parliamentary vote, 22 Conservative MPs and six DUP MPs voted against the government legislation.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:0d2-134) The vote ultimately passed by 515 votes to 29.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:0d2-134)
#### Immigration
Main article: [Rwanda asylum plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda_asylum_plan "Rwanda asylum plan")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Rishi_Sunak_holds_a_press_conference_on_the_Rwanda_asylum_plan%2C_22_April_2024.jpg/250px-Rishi_Sunak_holds_a_press_conference_on_the_Rwanda_asylum_plan%2C_22_April_2024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rishi_Sunak_holds_a_press_conference_on_the_Rwanda_asylum_plan,_22_April_2024.jpg)Sunak holds a press conference on the [Rwanda asylum plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda_asylum_plan "Rwanda asylum plan"), 22 April 2024. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_meets_Rwandan_President_Kagame_%2852870735268%29.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_meets_Rwandan_President_Kagame_%2852870735268%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_meets_Rwandan_President_Kagame_\(52870735268\).jpg)Sunak meeting Rwandan president [Paul Kagame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kagame "Paul Kagame") in Downing Street
In 2019 the Conservative Party and [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") pledged to reduce net migration below 250,000 per year, but Sunak said in 2023 that the priority was not to reduce legal immigration but to stop [illegal immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration_to_the_United_Kingdom "Illegal immigration to the United Kingdom").[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-135) Nearly 30,000 undocumented migrants crossed the Channel in small boats to the UK in 2023.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-136) Long-term [net migration to the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_immigration_to_the_United_Kingdom "Modern immigration to the United Kingdom") (the number of people immigrating minus the number emigrating) reached a record high of 764,000 in 2022,[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-137) with legal immigration at 1.26 million and emigration at 493,000.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-138) Of the 1,218,000 legal migrants coming to the UK in 2023, only 10% were EU Nationals.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-139)
Sunak continued the [Rwanda asylum plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda_asylum_plan "Rwanda asylum plan") to have asylum seekers and illegal immigrants sent to [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda") for processing.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-140)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-141) After the plan was blocked by the [UK's Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Appeal_\(England_and_Wales\) "Court of Appeal \(England and Wales\)") in June 2023 due to concerns over international law and the possibility of [refoulement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refoulement "Refoulement") (persecution of those sent to Rwanda), Sunak vowed to appeal against the verdict to the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_Kingdom "Supreme Court of the United Kingdom").[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-142)
On 15 November 2023, the Supreme Court upheld the ruling and declared the plan unlawful.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-143) In response, Sunak sent Cleverly to Rwanda to negotiate a treaty with Rwanda focused on preventing refoulement which must now be ratified by the British and Rwandan Parliaments.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-144) The government also introduced the [Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_of_Rwanda_\(Asylum_and_Immigration\)_Bill "Safety of Rwanda \(Asylum and Immigration\) Bill"), emergency legislation giving ministers the power to disapply sections of the [Human Rights Act 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Act_1998 "Human Rights Act 1998") and certain aspects of international law in order to allow them to declare Rwanda a safe country according to UK law.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-145) The bill was criticised by many on the right of the party for not going far enough, resulting in the resignation of the minister for immigration, Robert Jenrick.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-146)
On 12 December 2023 Sunak secured a government majority of 44 for the Safety of Rwanda Bill, despite the opposition of all other parties and abstentions from members of the [European Research Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Research_Group "European Research Group").[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-147)
#### Russia and Ukraine
Main article: [United Kingdom and the Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "United Kingdom and the Russian invasion of Ukraine")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_meets_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_-_52899900249.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_meets_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_-_52899900249.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_meets_Volodymyr_Zelenskyy_-_52899900249.jpg)Sunak with Ukrainian President [Volodymyr Zelenskyy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy "Volodymyr Zelenskyy") at [Chequers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chequers "Chequers"), May 2023
Following the [15 November missile explosion in Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_missile_explosion_in_Poland "2022 missile explosion in Poland"), Sunak met US President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and delivered a speech about it.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-148) Sunak later met Ukrainian President [Volodymyr Zelenskyy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy "Volodymyr Zelenskyy"), and pledged to give Ukraine £50 million in aid. After meeting Zelenskyy, Sunak said: "I am proud of how the [UK stood with Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "United Kingdom and the Russian invasion of Ukraine") from the very beginning. And I am here today to say the UK and our allies will continue to stand with Ukraine, as it fights to end this barbarous war and deliver a just peace."[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-149)
Sunak visited Ukraine on 12 January 2024 to sign a new U.K.-Ukraine Agreement on Security Cooperation with Zelenskyy promising £2.5 billion in military aid to Ukraine, including long-range missiles, artillery ammunition, air defence and maritime security, in addition to £200 million to be spent on military drones, making the UK the largest deliverer of drones to Ukraine out of any nation according to Downing Street.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:72-150)
#### Israel and Palestine
Main article: [United Kingdom support for Israel in the Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war "United Kingdom support for Israel in the Gaza war")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/The_Prime_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_of_Israel_%2853269898255%29.jpg/250px-The_Prime_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_of_Israel_%2853269898255%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Prime_Minister_meets_the_Prime_Minister_of_Israel_\(53269898255\).jpg)Sunak with Israeli prime minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu") in [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), 19 October 2023
In October 2023, Hamas [led a surprise attack on Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_October_attacks "7 October attacks") that [devolved into a war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war") and a growing [humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_humanitarian_crisis_\(2023%E2%80%93present\) "Gaza humanitarian crisis \(2023–present\)"). Sunak pledged the [UK's support for Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_support_for_Israel_in_the_Gaza_war "United Kingdom support for Israel in the Gaza war") and declared that Israel "has an absolute right to defend itself".[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:82-151) Sunak backed calls for humanitarian pauses to allow for aid to be brought into Gaza, although he initially rejected calls for a full ceasefire as he argued that this would only benefit Hamas.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:92-152)
Israel used British-supplied weapons in the war.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-153)[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-154) However, Sunak later condemned the high number of [civilian casualties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casualties_of_the_Gaza_war "Casualties of the Gaza war") in Gaza and called for a "sustainable ceasefire" in which all Israeli hostages were returned to Israel, attacks against Israel ceased and humanitarian aid was allowed into Gaza.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:102-155) His government supported the [two-state solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-state_solution "Two-state solution") as a resolution to the conflict.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-156)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-157)
When the [International Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court "International Criminal Court") prosecutor [Karim Ahmad Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karim_Ahmad_Khan "Karim Ahmad Khan") announced that he would seek to charge Israeli prime minister [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu") with war crimes, Sunak criticised the move as "unhelpful" and accused Khan of drawing a moral equivalence between Israel and Hamas.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-158)
### Local election results
See also: [2023 United Kingdom local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2023 United Kingdom local elections"), [2024 United Kingdom local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2024 United Kingdom local elections"), and [Leadership approval opinion polling for the 2024 United Kingdom general election § Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_approval_opinion_polling_for_the_2024_United_Kingdom_general_election#Rishi_Sunak "Leadership approval opinion polling for the 2024 United Kingdom general election")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Prime_Minister_campaigns_in_Selby_%2853031710063%29.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_campaigns_in_Selby_%2853031710063%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_campaigns_in_Selby_\(53031710063\).jpg)Sunak campaigning in July 2023
Sunak was faced with the task of rebuilding the Conservatives' reputation which had been significantly damaged by the [controversies and scandals of the previous year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Boris_Johnson#Scandals "Premiership of Boris Johnson") and the Truss ministry. While their poll ratings recovered slightly over the following months, it still wasn't enough to bring them back to pre-Truss levels. Sunak contested his first [local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2023 United Kingdom local elections") as leader on 4 May 2023, where the Conservatives suffered heavy losses. Two months later, on 20 July 2023, they lost two seats in by-elections; [one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Selby_and_Ainsty_by-election "2023 Selby and Ainsty by-election") to Labour and [one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerton_and_Frome_\(UK_Parliament_constituency\) "Somerton and Frome \(UK Parliament constituency\)") to the Liberal Democrats. Their fortunes remained unchanged throughout policy changes of the following year, such as the shelving of the [HS2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HS2 "HS2") northern phase in October. The Conservatives lost two further seats in by-elections on 15 February 2024.
In March 2024, there were suggestions that Sunak could face a leadership challenge before the upcoming [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election") — which was expected within the calendar year — if the Conservatives perform poorly at the [local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2024 United Kingdom local elections") on 2 May.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-159)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-160)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-161) Sunak however said he would resist a challenge, even if that ends up being the case.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-162)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-163) As predicted, 2 May saw grim showing for the Conservatives, who suffered their worst local election results since [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_Kingdom_local_elections "1996 United Kingdom local elections"). Additionally, they lost another seat to Labour in the [Blackpool South by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpool_South_by-election "Blackpool South by-election"), and narrowly lost the [West Midlands mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_West_Midlands_mayoral_election "2024 West Midlands mayoral election") in a knife-edge vote. Sunak's premiership was described as more stable than that of his two predecessors, while still not being able to represent a turnaround for the Conservatives.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-164)
### 2024 general election and resignation
Main article: [2024 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_leaves_10_Downing_Street_%2853836890030%29.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_leaves_10_Downing_Street_%2853836890030%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_leaves_10_Downing_Street_\(53836890030\).jpg)Sunak delivers speech before leaving 10 Downing Street in July 2024 
On the afternoon of 22 May 2024, Sunak announced that he had asked the King to call a general election for 4 July 2024, surprising his own MPs.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-165) Though Sunak had the option to wait until December 2024 to call the election, he said that he decided on the date because he believed that the economy was improving, and that "falling inflation and net migration figures would reinforce the Conservatives' election message of 'sticking to the plan'".[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-166)
Sunak sought to rebuild the Conservative's reputation following a slump in popularity after the short-lived Truss ministry and a slew of controversies including Partygate that irreparably damaged Johnson's ministry,[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-167) through campaigning on stabilising the economy, the Rwanda asylum plan, further strengthening the [State Pension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Pension "State Pension"), and introducing [National Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_the_United_Kingdom#Support_for_reintroduction_of_conscription "Conscription in the United Kingdom"). He released the Conservative manifesto _[Clear Plan. Bold Action. Secure Future.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear_Plan._Bold_Action._Secure_Future. "Clear Plan. Bold Action. Secure Future.")_ on 11 June, addressing the economy, taxes, welfare, expanding free childcare, education, healthcare, environment, energy, transport, and crime.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-168)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-169) Sunak stated during the general election campaign that if his party lost the election he intended to remain as a backbench MP for the next 5 years.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-170) On 6 June 2024, the 80th anniversary of [D-Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-Day "D-Day"), Sunak was heavily criticised for leaving commemoration events early to do an interview with ITV,[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-171)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-172)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-173) including by veterans.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-174)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-175) Sunak apologised three times over the following week.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-176)
Labour won a landslide victory in the general election, ending 14 years of Conservative government. A record number of Conservative MPs either [stood down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_MPs_who_stood_down_at_the_2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "List of MPs who stood down at the 2024 United Kingdom general election") or [lost their seats at the election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_MPs_who_lost_their_seat_in_the_2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "List of MPs who lost their seat in the 2024 United Kingdom general election"). Three Cabinet members stood down and eight full members and four who attended Cabinet lost their seats, the highest number of sitting cabinet seat losses in history.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-177) Sunak conceded the election on 5 July. In his resignation speech before tending his resignation to the King, Sunak apologised to Conservative voters and candidates for the party's heavy defeat, and announced his intention to resign as party leader once a new leader is elected. He also offered support to the incoming prime minister [Keir Starmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer "Keir Starmer"), saying he was "a decent, public-spirited man" he respected and expressed hope he would be successful.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-178)[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-179)
> To all the Conservative candidates and campaigners who worked tirelessly but without success, I am sorry that we could not deliver what your efforts deserved. It pains me to think how many good colleagues, who contributed so much to their communities and our country, will now no longer sit in the House of Commons. I thank them for their hard work, and their service. Following this result, I will step down as party leader, not immediately, but once the formal arrangements for selecting my successor are in place. It is important that after 14 years in government the Conservative Party rebuilds, but also that it takes up its crucial role in Opposition professionally and effectively.
## Post-premiership (2024–present)
### Leader of the Opposition (July–November 2024)
Main article: [Shadow Cabinet of Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Rishi_Sunak "Shadow Cabinet of Rishi Sunak")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_leaves_10_Downing_Street_%2853836772719%29.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_leaves_10_Downing_Street_%2853836772719%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_leaves_10_Downing_Street_\(53836772719\).jpg)Sunak and his wife, [Akshata Murty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akshata_Murty "Akshata Murty"), leaving [Downing Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downing_Street "Downing Street")
After Starmer succeeded Sunak as prime minister, Sunak immediately became [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_\(United_Kingdom\) "Leader of the Opposition \(United Kingdom\)") and formed his [shadow cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Rishi_Sunak "Shadow Cabinet of Rishi Sunak") on 8 July.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-LBC2-180)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:03-181)
Most members of Sunak's cabinet heading into the 2024 general election were given the same portfolios in the shadow cabinet, including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, who became [shadow chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_chancellor "Shadow chancellor"), and former home secretary James Cleverly, who became [shadow home secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_home_secretary "Shadow home secretary").[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:03-181) Former foreign secretary David Cameron chose to retire from frontline politics, with his former deputy [Andrew Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Mitchell "Andrew Mitchell") becoming [shadow foreign secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_foreign_secretary "Shadow foreign secretary") instead.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-182) Richard Holden resigned as [party chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Conservative_Party "Chairman of the Conservative Party"), and was succeeded by [Richard Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Fuller_\(Conservative_politician\) "Richard Fuller \(Conservative politician\)") in an interim capacity outside shadow cabinet.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:13-183)
Sunak appointed new officeholders to the portfolios held by the eleven cabinet ministers who lost their seats in the election, including [Edward Argar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Argar "Edward Argar"), who became [shadow justice secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_Justice "Shadow Secretary of State for Justice") after the outgoing justice secretary [Alex Chalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Chalk "Alex Chalk") lost his seat, as well as [Helen Whately](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Whately "Helen Whately"), who became [shadow transport secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_transport_secretary "Shadow transport secretary") after the outgoing transport secretary [Mark Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Harper "Mark Harper") also lost his seat.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-LBC2-180) Among other noteworthy appointments, [Kemi Badenoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemi_Badenoch "Kemi Badenoch") became the [shadow housing, communities and local government secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_Housing,_Communities_and_Local_Government "Shadow Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government") and former deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden became [deputy leader of the opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Opposition_\(United_Kingdom\) "Deputy Leader of the Opposition \(United Kingdom\)").[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-LBC2-180)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:13-183)
Sunak remained leader until his successor, Kemi Badenoch, was elected in the [2024 Conservative Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Conservative_Party_leadership_election "2024 Conservative Party leadership election"),[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-184)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-185) after which he returned to the backbenches. Responding to the [2024 State Opening of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_State_Opening_of_Parliament "2024 State Opening of Parliament"), Sunak said his party would not oppose the government "for the sake of it", but would hold them to account on their election promises. On proposals to change planning laws, Sunak said that though such changes were needed "a system that does not allow local people to have a say will damage public consent for more housing in the long term".[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Growth-186) While he respected Starmer's decision to scrap the Rwanda asylum plan, Sunak said that there needed to be an alternative deterrent, otherwise "a large number of those who crossed the Channel illegally will end up remaining here".[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Hardman-187)
In that same speech, Sunak summarized the rapid trajectory of his political career:
> On the Government benches life comes at you fast.
> Soon, you might be fortunate enough to be tapped on the shoulder and be offered a junior ministerial role, then you'll find yourself attending cabinet, then in the cabinet and then when the prime minister's position becomes untenable you might end up being called to the highest office.
> And, before you know it, you have a bright future behind you and you're left wondering whether you can credibly be an elder statesman at the age of 44.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Hardman-187)
### Other activities
In January 2025, he became a visiting fellow at the [Hoover Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoover_Institution "Hoover Institution") of [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"),[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Telegraph_Hoover-188) a distinguished fellow at the [Blavatnik School of Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blavatnik_School_of_Government "Blavatnik School of Government")[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-189)[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-190) and signed as an exclusive speaker with the [Washington Speakers Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Speakers_Bureau "Washington Speakers Bureau").[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-191) In March 2025, Sunak and his wife [Akshata Murty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akshata_Murty "Akshata Murty") founded a charity called The Richmond Project which aims to improve the numeracy skills of schoolchildren and adults.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-192)
In July 2025, Sunak took up a position as a senior adviser at [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"). With this appointment, [ACOBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACOBA "ACOBA") restricted him for a year from lobbying the government and influencing policy, and advising [investment funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_funds "Investment funds") and foreign governments.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-193)
Sunak became a paid advisor to both [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") and artificial intelligence start-up [Anthropic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropic "Anthropic") in October 2025; the appointments were again subject to ACOBA restrictions.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-MicrosoftOct25-194) Sunak stated he would donate his earnings from the roles to a charity he had founded.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-MicrosoftOct25-194)
## Political positions
Main article: [Political positions of Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_positions_of_Rishi_Sunak "Political positions of Rishi Sunak")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Levelling_up_-_Sunak_and_Hunt.jpg/250px-Levelling_up_-_Sunak_and_Hunt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Levelling_up_-_Sunak_and_Hunt.jpg)Sunak and [Jeremy Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hunt "Jeremy Hunt") holding a [Levelling Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levelling-up_policy_of_the_Conservative_government "Levelling-up policy of the Conservative government") sign, January 2023
Sunak has been described as a moderate within his party with a [technocratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technocratic "Technocratic") or managerial leadership style.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-195) According to [Euronews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euronews "Euronews"), Sunak is "frequently perceived as a pragmatist and as belonging to the centre-ground of the Conservative Party".[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Carlo-20222-196) He opposed [the economic policies of Truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trussonomics "Trussonomics"),[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Carlo-20222-196) and although described as a fellow [Thatcherite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thatcherite "Thatcherite"), he is viewed as less [economically liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economically_liberal "Economically liberal") than Truss.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Dutton-20222-197)
In April 2023, Sunak's perception as a centrist contrasted with descriptions of his government's policies on transgender and migration issues as being [socially conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socially_conservative "Socially conservative"), with Jessica Elgot of _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_ describing Sunak as "perhaps the most socially conservative PM of his generation".[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-198) Robert Shrimsley of the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times")_ described Sunak as someone whose "easy manner, career in global finance and ethnic background might suggest a more cosmopolitan conservative", even though he is socially conservative and pragmatic.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-199) Meanwhile, the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Statesman "New Statesman")_ described Sunak as uneasily straddling both [liberal-conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal-conservative "Liberal-conservative") and [national-conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National-conservative "National-conservative") instincts.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-200) In July 2023, _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Economist "The Economist")_ described him as "the most right-wing Conservative prime minister since [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher")".[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-201)
## Public image
Following his appointment as chancellor, Sunak arrived in public discourse from relative obscurity.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Sharma-2020-202) Some political commentators saw Sunak's appointment as signalling the end of the Treasury's independence from Downing Street, with Robert Shrimsley, chief political commentator of the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times")_ , arguing that "good government often depends on senior ministers – and the Chancellor in particular – being able to fight bad ideas".[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-203)
In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, he was popular by the standards of British politics, described by one analyst as having "better ratings than any politician since the heydays of Tony Blair".[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Walker-2022a-204) Various polls showed Sunak remained overwhelmingly popular among Conservative supporters and many other Britons throughout 2020.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-205)[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-206)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-207) In an [Ipsos MORI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipsos_MORI "Ipsos MORI") poll in September 2020, Sunak had the highest satisfaction score of any British chancellor since Labour's Denis Healey in April 1978, and was widely seen as the favourite to become the next Conservative leader.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-208)[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-209) Sunak developed a [cult media following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following"), with jokes and gossip about his attractiveness widespread on social media and in magazines, gaining the nickname "Dishy Rishi".[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Sharma-2020-202)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-210)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Walker-2022a-204)[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-211)
Public attitudes towards Sunak remained broadly positive in 2021,[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-212)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-213)[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-214) though his popularity declined steadily over time.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Walker-2022a-204) By early 2022, with the cost of living becoming a growing focus of public concern, Sunak's response as chancellor was perceived as inadequate and he received some of his lowest approval ratings, which continued as the Sunak family's financial affairs came under scrutiny.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-215)[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-216)[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-217)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-218)[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-219) By the time he resigned as chancellor in July 2022, Sunak's approval ratings slightly recovered.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-220) In October 2022, following his appointment as prime minister, Sunak's personal favourability ratings increased.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-221)[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-222) By July 2023, Sunak's approval ratings had decreased back to a similar level to when he resigned as chancellor.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-223) The _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Statesman "New Statesman")_ named him as the second most powerful right-wing figure of 2023, behind only [Nigel Farage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Farage "Nigel Farage").[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:1-224) By his resignation as prime minister in July 2024, he had his lowest approval ratings to date.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-225) Following the 2024 general election, Sunak received praise for being gracious in defeat, with some commentators recommending for the Conservatives to keep him on as leader.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-226)[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-227)
## Personal life
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Trooping_the_Colour_2024_%28GovPM_09%29.jpg/250px-Trooping_the_Colour_2024_%28GovPM_09%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trooping_the_Colour_2024_\(GovPM_09\).jpg)The Sunak family in Downing Street (on the [King's Official Birthday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Official_Birthday "King's Official Birthday"), 15 June 2024). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_attends_Coronation_Big_Lunch_%2852877779154%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_attends_Coronation_Big_Lunch_%2852877779154%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Rishi_Sunak_attends_Coronation_Big_Lunch_\(52877779154\)_\(cropped\).jpg)Sunak with his family celebrating the [Coronation of Charles III and Camilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_Charles_III_and_Camilla "Coronation of Charles III and Camilla"), May 2023
In August 2009, Sunak married [Akshata Murty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akshata_Murty "Akshata Murty"), the daughter of [N. R. Narayana Murthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N._R._Narayana_Murthy "N. R. Narayana Murthy") and [Sudha Murty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudha_Murty "Sudha Murty"). His father-in-law is the founder of the technology company [Infosys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infosys "Infosys"), in which Murty owns a stake,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Telegraph-22)[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-228) while his mother-in-law is a prolific Indian author and educator.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-229) Sunak and Murty met while studying at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in the US, and he proposed to her on a cliff near the [Ritz-Carlton Half Moon Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritz-Carlton_Half_Moon_Bay "Ritz-Carlton Half Moon Bay").[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Ross-230) They have two daughters: the first born in 2011 and the second in 2013.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Telegraph-22)[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-econindia-231) In November 2020, Sunak was reported by _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_ to have not declared a significant amount of his wife and family's financial interests on the register of ministers' interests, including a combined £1.7 billion shareholding in Infosys. Ministers are required to declare interests that are "relevant" to their responsibilities and "which might be thought to give rise to a conflict" with their public duties.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Gintersts-232) The independent adviser on ministers' interests investigated and concluded that Sunak had not broken any rules.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-233)[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-234)
In early 2022, newspapers reported that Murty had [non-domiciled status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_with_non-domiciled_status_in_the_UK "List of people with non-domiciled status in the UK"), meaning she did not have to pay [tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxation_in_the_United_Kingdom "Taxation in the United Kingdom") on income earned abroad while living in the UK.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Walker-2022b-235) The status cost approximately £30,000 to secure, and allowed her to avoid paying an estimated £20 million in UK taxes.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Walker-2022b-235)[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-236) On 8 April Murty issued a statement saying that she would pay UK taxes on her global income, and that she regretted the issue had become "a distraction for [her] husband". An inquiry was set up to identify the source of the leak regarding her tax status.[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-237) Reporting around this time also revealed that Sunak had continued to hold United States' [permanent resident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_card "Green card") (green card) status he had acquired in the 2000s until 2021, including for 18 months after he was made chancellor, which required filing annual US tax returns.[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-238)[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-239) An investigation into both his wife's tax status and his residency status found that Sunak had not broken any ministerial rules.[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-240)
Sunak and Murty live in [Kirby Sigston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirby_Sigston "Kirby Sigston"), near [Northallerton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northallerton "Northallerton"), North Yorkshire.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-241) They own several other homes, including a [mews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mews "Mews") house in [Earl's Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl's_Court "Earl's Court") in central London; a flat on the [Old Brompton Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Brompton_Road "Old Brompton Road") in [South Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kensington "South Kensington"); and a penthouse apartment on [Ocean Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Avenue_\(Santa_Monica\) "Ocean Avenue \(Santa Monica\)") in [Santa Monica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica,_California "Santa Monica, California"), California.[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-242)[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-243)[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-244)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Edwardes-12)[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-observer-20220403-245) In April 2022, it was reported that Sunak and Murty had moved out of the flat above 10 Downing Street to a newly refurbished west London home for domestic reasons.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-246)[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-247) In October 2022, the Sunaks resumed residence of their former official home at 10 Downing Street, this time as prime minister and reversing the trend started in 1997 of prime ministers living in the four-bedroom flat above [11 Downing Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11_Downing_Street "11 Downing Street").[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-248)[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-249)[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-250) In August 2023, Sunak and his family quietly left the UK for 10 days in Santa Monica for his first holiday in almost four years, where they visited the [Santa Monica Pier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_Pier "Santa Monica Pier") and [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland "Disneyland"), and attended one of the concerts of [The Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") by [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift").[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Landler-251)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Sue_Gray_report_Fig_3_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Sue_Gray_report_Fig_3_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sue_Gray_report_Fig_3_\(cropped\).jpg)Sunak at the gathering on Johnson's birthday that breached COVID-19 regulations, June 2020
In April 2022, amid the [Partygate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partygate "Partygate") scandal, Sunak was issued a [fixed penalty notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_penalty_notice "Fixed penalty notice") by the police who believed he had committed offences under COVID-19 regulations by attending a birthday gathering for Boris Johnson on 19 June 2020. The police also issued 125 fixed penalty notices to 82 other individuals, including Johnson and his wife [Carrie Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrie_Symonds "Carrie Symonds"), who all apologised and paid the penalties.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-252)[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-253) After receiving the penalty notice, Sunak said he was "extremely and sincerely sorry" for the hurt caused by him attending the party, and that he respected the police's decision to give him a fine.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-254) In January 2023, Sunak was issued a fixed penalty notice by [Lancashire Constabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_Constabulary "Lancashire Constabulary") after a social media video of him failing to wear a [seat belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seat_belt "Seat belt") in a moving vehicle was published.[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-:2-255) After Johnson, he became the second Prime Minister found to have broken the law in office.[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-256) Sunak apologised for the incident and said he made a "brief error of judgment".[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-257)
Sunak is a [teetotaller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teetotaller "Teetotaller").[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-258) He stated in 2022 that he had seven dental fillings due to excessive consumption of [Coca-Cola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca-Cola "Coca-Cola") when he was younger, and expressed a strong preference for [Mexican Coke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Coke "Mexican Coke").[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-259) He was previously a governor of the [East London Science School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London_Science_School "East London Science School").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-PE-36) Sunak has a [Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Retriever "Labrador Retriever") called Nova and is a cricket and horse racing enthusiast.[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Roberts-260)[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-261)[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-262) As chancellor, Sunak rose early for a daily [Peloton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloton_Interactive "Peloton Interactive") workout and was a fan of fitness instructor [Cody Rigsby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cody_Rigsby "Cody Rigsby"). Sunak is a close friend of _[The Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator "The Spectator")_ 's former political editor [James Forsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Forsyth_\(journalist\) "James Forsyth \(journalist\)"), whom he has known since their school days. Sunak was the best man at Forsyth's wedding to the journalist [Allegra Stratton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegra_Stratton "Allegra Stratton"), and they are godparents to each other's children.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Edwardes-12) He appointed Forsyth as his political secretary in December 2022.[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-263)
Sunak is a steadfast [Southampton F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton_F.C. "Southampton F.C.") fan.[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-264)[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-265) When asked what his ideal job would be if he was not a politician, he replied that if he could "run Southampton Football Club" he would be a "very happy man".[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-The_Independent-266)
Sunak is a Hindu and identifies as [British-Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indians "British Indians"), stating that he is "thoroughly British" but with an Indian religious and cultural heritage.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Business2-18) He took his oath as an MP at the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") on the _[Bhagavad Gita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhagavad_Gita "Bhagavad Gita")_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Business2-18)[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-267)[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-268) During the [coronation of Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_Charles_III "Coronation of Charles III"), Sunak gave a reading from the [Epistle to the Colossians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Colossians "Epistle to the Colossians") – Colossians 1:9–17.[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-269)[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-270) After the [murder of George Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd") by police officer [Derek Chauvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Chauvin "Derek Chauvin"), Sunak said he had also faced racism in his life.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-Dutton-20222-197)
Speaking about his childhood during the 2024 general election campaign, Sunak said his parents "wanted to put everything into our education and that was a priority" and that he did not have [Sky TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_UK "Sky UK") growing up.[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak#cite_note-271)
